exercises.title: Your First HTML Page
exercises.description: Create a basic HTML page with the required document structure.
exercises.instructions:
Every HTML page needs a basic structure to work properly. Create a valid HTML5 page by adding the required elements.

Your page should have:
- A `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration at the very top
- An `<html>` element with `lang="en"`
- A `<head>` section
- A `<body>` section

This is the skeleton that every web page is built on.

<!-- Add the DOCTYPE declaration -->

<!-- Add the html element with lang="en" -->

  <!-- Add the head section -->

  <!-- Add the body section -->
exercises.solution:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
hints: Every HTML page starts with a special declaration that tells the browser what version of HTML you are using. What does that declaration look like?
The structure is: DOCTYPE at the top, then an <html> element that contains both a <head> and a <body> section.

exercises.title: Page Title
exercises.description: Add a title to your HTML page that appears in the browser tab.
exercises.instructions:
The `<title>` element sets the text that appears in the browser tab. It must be placed inside the `<head>` section.

Add a `<title>` element inside the `<head>` with the text "My First Page".

Example: When you open a website, the text you see on the browser tab is the page title.
exercises.starterCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <!-- Add a title element with the text "My First Page" -->

  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
exercises.solution:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>My First Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
hints: There is a specific HTML element that controls what text appears in the browser tab. Where should it be placed — in the head or the body?
The <title> element goes inside the <head> section. The text you want displayed goes between the opening and closing title tags.

exercises.title: Head and Body
exercises.description: Add a title in the head and a heading in the body of an HTML page.
exercises.instructions:
The `<head>` contains information about the page (like the title). The `<body>` contains what visitors actually see.

Add:
- A `<title>` element inside `<head>` with the text "Hello World"
- An `<h1>` element inside `<body>` with the text "Welcome!"

Remember: The head is for the browser, the body is for the viewer.

  <body>
    <!-- Add an h1 heading with "Welcome!" -->

  </body>
</html>
exercises.solution: Welcome!
hints: The page has two main sections. One holds information the browser uses behind the scenes, and the other holds content the visitor sees on screen.
Use <title> inside <head> for the tab text. Use <h1> inside <body> for the visible heading.

exercises.title: Heading Levels
exercises.description: Use heading elements h1 through h3 to create a content hierarchy.
exercises.instructions:
HTML has six levels of headings, from `<h1>` (most important) to `<h6>` (least important). They create a visual and structural hierarchy for your content.

Add the following headings in order:
- An `<h1>` with "Main Title"
- An `<h2>` with "Section Title"
- An `<h3>` with "Subsection Title"

Every page should have exactly one `<h1>`. Use `<h2>` through `<h6>` for subsections.

Use <h1> for the most important heading, <h2> for the next level, and <h3> for the level after that. Each has an opening and closing tag.

exercises.description: Use strong and em elements to add emphasis to text.
exercises.instructions:
HTML provides elements to add emphasis to text:
- `<strong>` makes text **bold** — use it for important content
- `<em>` makes text *italic* — use it for stressed emphasis

Create a paragraph that contains:
- The word "important" wrapped in `<strong>` tags
- The word "really" wrapped in `<em>` tags

The full text should read: "This is really important information."

hints: There are two HTML elements that change how text looks and what it means to screen readers. One makes text bold, the other italic.

exercises.title: Unordered List
exercises.description: Create a bulleted list using ul and li elements.
exercises.instructions:
An unordered list displays items with bullet points. It uses two elements:
- `<ul>` — the list container (unordered list)
- `<li>` — each item in the list (list item)

Create an unordered list with three items:
- "Apples"
- "Bananas"
- "Oranges"

Every `<li>` must be inside a `<ul>` to work correctly.
exercises.solution:
• Apples
  • Bananas
  • Oranges
hints: An unordered list needs a container element and individual item elements inside it. What are the HTML tags for these?
The container is <ul> (unordered list). Each item uses <li> (list item) with the text between opening and closing tags.

exercises.title: Ordered List
exercises.description: Create a numbered list using ol and li elements.
exercises.instructions:
An ordered list displays items with numbers. It uses `<ol>` instead of `<ul>`, but the items still use `<li>`.

Create an ordered list with three steps:
1. "Preheat the oven"
2. "Mix the ingredients"
3. "Bake for 30 minutes"

The browser automatically numbers each item for you.
exercises.solution:
1. Preheat the oven
  2. Mix the ingredients
  3. Bake for 30 minutes
hints: A numbered list works just like a bulleted list, but uses a different container element. What tag creates a numbered (ordered) list?
Change <ul> to <ol> for ordered lists. The <li> elements stay the same — the browser handles the numbering automatically.

Use <h2> for the heading. Then create a <ul> with five or more <li> elements, each containing a grocery item.

exercises.title: Simple Table
exercises.description: Create a basic 2-column table with 3 rows of data.
exercises.instructions:
Tables use three main elements:
- `<table>` — the table container
- `<tr>` — a table row
- `<td>` — a table data cell

Create a table with 3 rows and 2 columns:
- Row 1: "Name" and "Age"
- Row 2: "Alex" and "25"
- Row 3: "Sam" and "30"

Each `<td>` goes inside a `<tr>`, and all `<tr>` elements go inside `<table>`.

Name Age
Alex 25
Sam 30

Use <tr> for each row and <td> for each cell within that row. Nest them inside a <table> element.

exercises.description: Use th elements to create bold header cells in a table.

Create a table with:
- A header row using `<th>` with "Product" and "Price"
- Two data rows using `<td>`:

  - "Tea" and "$2.50"

Tea $2.50

Product Price

Tea $2.50

Replace <td> with <th> for the first row to create header cells. Data rows still use <td>.

exercises.title: Table Sections
exercises.description: Organize a table into head, body, and foot sections.
exercises.instructions:

- `<thead>` — the header section (column labels)
- `<tbody>` — the body section (data rows)
- `<tfoot>` — the footer section (summary row)

Create a table with:
- `<thead>` containing a row with `<th>` cells: "Item" and "Cost"
- `<tbody>` containing two rows: "Lunch" / "$12" and "Dinner" / "$25"
- `<tfoot>` containing a row: "Total" and "$37"

Item Cost

Wrap your header row in <thead>, your data rows in <tbody>, and your summary row in <tfoot>. Each section still uses <tr> and <td>/<th> inside.

2. Reassign `count` to `count + 10`
3. Declare a `const` called `label` and assign it `"Total: " + count`

After running, `count` should be `11` and `label` should be `"Total: 11"`.
hints: You can change a `let` variable by writing just the name, equals, and new value — no keyword needed for reassignment.
Write `let count = 1;` then `count = count + 10;` then `const label = "Total: " + count;`.

exercises.title: Declare a Variable
exercises.description: Use let to declare a variable and assign it a value.
exercises.instructions:
Variables store data that your program can use later. In JavaScript, you declare a variable with `let` and assign a value with `=`.

Declare a variable called `greeting` using `let` and assign it the string `"Hello, World!"`.

Then return `greeting` from the function.

Example: `let age = 25;` declares a variable named `age` with the value `25`.
hints: Variables in JavaScript are created using a keyword followed by the variable name, an equals sign, and the value.
Use `let` followed by the variable name, then `=` and the string value in quotes. Use `return` to send the value back.

exercises.title: Constants
exercises.description: Use const to declare a value that should not change.
exercises.instructions:
When a value should never change, use `const` instead of `let`. Trying to reassign a `const` variable will cause an error.

Declare a constant called `PI` with the value `3.14159` and return it.

Use `const` for values that stay the same throughout your program — it makes your code safer and easier to understand.
hints: There is a keyword for declaring variables whose values should never be reassigned after creation.
Use `const` instead of `let` when the value should not change. The syntax is the same: `const NAME = value;`.

exercises.title: String Variable
exercises.description: Store a name in a variable and return it.
exercises.instructions:
Strings are text values wrapped in quotes. You can use single quotes (`'...'`), double quotes (`"..."`), or backticks (`` `...` ``).

Write a function that stores the name `"CodeForge"` in a variable called `appName` and returns it.

Strings are one of the most common data types in programming.
hints: Text values in JavaScript must be wrapped in some kind of quote marks to create a string.
Declare a variable with `let` or `const`, assign it a string value in quotes, then use `return` to send it back.

exercises.title: Number Variable
exercises.description: Store a number in a variable and use it in a calculation.
exercises.instructions:
Numbers in JavaScript are written without quotes. You can use them directly in math operations.

Write a function that stores the number `10` in a variable called `width` and `5` in a variable called `height`, then returns their product (width times height).

This is how you use variables to perform calculations.
hints: Numbers are written without quotes. The multiplication operator in JavaScript is an asterisk.
Declare two variables with their numeric values, then return the result of multiplying them using the `*` operator.

exercises.title: Boolean Variable
exercises.description: Store a true or false value in a variable.
exercises.instructions:
Booleans represent one of two values: `true` or `false`. They are used to make decisions in your code.

Write a function that takes a parameter `age` and returns `true` if the age is 18 or greater, or `false` otherwise.

Store the result in a variable called `isAdult` before returning it.

Example: `canVote(21)` should return `true`, `canVote(15)` should return `false`.
hints: Comparison operators like `>=` automatically produce a boolean result — either `true` or `false`.
Store the result of `age >= 18` in a variable. The expression itself evaluates to a boolean.

exercises.title: Variable Reassignment
exercises.description: Change the value of a let variable after declaring it.
exercises.instructions:
Variables declared with `let` can have their values changed (reassigned). Variables declared with `const` cannot.

Write a function that declares a variable `score` with `let`, sets it to `0`, then adds `10` to it, then adds `5` more. Return the final value.

Reassignment uses `=` without the `let` keyword.
hints: After declaring a variable with `let`, you can change its value by writing the variable name, `=`, and the new value — without repeating `let`.
Start with `let score = 0;` then reassign: `score = score + 10;` adds 10 to the current value.

exercises.title: Typeof
exercises.description: Use typeof to check what type a value is.
exercises.instructions:
The `typeof` operator returns a string telling you what type a value is. It works with any value.

Write a function `checkType(value)` that returns the result of `typeof value`.

Examples:
- `checkType(42)` returns `"number"`
- `checkType("hello")` returns `"string"`
- `checkType(true)` returns `"boolean"`
hints: JavaScript has an operator that tells you the data type of any value. It returns the type as a string.
Use `typeof` before the value or variable: `typeof value`. It returns a string like `"number"` or `"string"`.

exercises.title: Null and Undefined
exercises.description: Understand the difference between null and undefined.
exercises.instructions:
`undefined` means a variable has been declared but not assigned a value. `null` means a variable has been intentionally set to "no value."

Write a function `checkEmpty(value)` that returns:
- `"undefined"` if the value is `undefined`
- `"null"` if the value is `null`
- `"has value"` if the value is anything else

Use `===` to check for exact matches.
hints: You can compare a value to `undefined` or `null` directly using the strict equality operator.
Use `if (value === undefined)` and `if (value === null)` to check each case. Use `===` not `==` to avoid type coercion.

resources.label: W3Schools: JavaScript Data Types
resources.description: JavaScript data types including null and undefined

exercises.title: Addition and Subtraction
exercises.description: Write expressions using the addition and subtraction operators.
exercises.instructions:
The `+` operator adds numbers and the `-` operator subtracts them.

Write a function `addAndSubtract(a, b, c)` that returns the result of `a + b - c`.

Examples:
- `addAndSubtract(10, 5, 3)` returns `12`
- `addAndSubtract(100, 50, 25)` returns `125`
hints: The `+` symbol adds two values and the `-` symbol subtracts one value from another.
Combine both operators in one expression: `a + b - c`. Store or return the result directly.

exercises.title: Multiplication and Division
exercises.description: Write expressions using the multiplication and division operators.
exercises.instructions:
The `*` operator multiplies numbers and the `/` operator divides them.

Write a function `calculateAverage(a, b)` that returns the average of two numbers. The average is calculated by adding the numbers and dividing by 2.

Examples:
- `calculateAverage(10, 20)` returns `15`
- `calculateAverage(7, 3)` returns `5`
hints: To get an average, first add the two values together, then divide the total by how many values there are.
Use parentheses to control the order: `(a + b) / 2` ensures the addition happens before the division.

exercises.title: Modulo
exercises.description: Use the modulo operator to find remainders.
exercises.instructions:
The modulo operator (`%`) returns the remainder after division. It is useful for checking divisibility.

Write a function `getRemainder(a, b)` that returns the remainder when `a` is divided by `b`.

Examples:
- `getRemainder(10, 3)` returns `1` (10 divided by 3 is 3 remainder 1)
- `getRemainder(20, 5)` returns `0` (20 divides evenly by 5)
hints: There is an operator that gives you the leftover amount after dividing two numbers.
The `%` operator returns the remainder. Use `a % b` to get what is left over after dividing `a` by `b`.

exercises.title: Comparison Operators
exercises.description: Use comparison operators to compare two values.
exercises.instructions:
Comparison operators compare two values and return `true` or `false`:
- `>` greater than
- `<` less than
- `>=` greater than or equal to
- `<=` less than or equal to

Write a function `isGreater(a, b)` that returns `true` if `a` is greater than `b`, otherwise `false`.

Examples:
- `isGreater(10, 5)` returns `true`
- `isGreater(3, 7)` returns `false`
hints: Comparison operators produce boolean results automatically — you do not need an if statement.
The expression `a > b` already evaluates to `true` or `false`. You can return it directly.

exercises.title: Strict Equality
exercises.description: Use strict equality to check if two values are exactly equal.
exercises.instructions:
The strict equality operator (`===`) checks if two values are equal in both value and type. The strict inequality operator (`!==`) checks if they are not equal.

Write a function `isExactMatch(a, b)` that returns `true` if `a` and `b` are strictly equal, otherwise `false`.

Always use `===` instead of `==` — strict equality prevents surprising type conversion bugs.

Examples:
- `isExactMatch(5, 5)` returns `true`
- `isExactMatch(5, "5")` returns `false` (number vs string)
hints: JavaScript has two equality operators. One checks value only, the other checks both value and type.
Use `===` (three equals signs) to compare both the value and the type. The expression returns `true` or `false`.

exercises.title: Logical AND/OR
exercises.description: Combine conditions using logical AND and OR operators.
exercises.instructions:
Logical operators combine boolean values:
- `&&` (AND) — returns `true` only if both sides are `true`
- `||` (OR) — returns `true` if at least one side is `true`

Write a function `canRideRollercoaster(age, height)` that returns `true` if the person is at least 12 years old AND at least 48 inches tall.

Examples:
- `canRideRollercoaster(14, 52)` returns `true`
- `canRideRollercoaster(10, 52)` returns `false` (too young)
hints: When you need both conditions to be true at the same time, there is a logical operator that combines them.
Use `&&` between two comparison expressions. Both sides must be `true` for the whole expression to be `true`.

exercises.title: Logical NOT
exercises.description: Negate a condition using the logical NOT operator.
exercises.instructions:
The logical NOT operator (`!`) flips a boolean value — `true` becomes `false` and `false` becomes `true`.

Write a function `isNotEmpty(str)` that returns `true` if the string's length is NOT zero, otherwise `false`.

Examples:
- `isNotEmpty("hello")` returns `true`
- `isNotEmpty("")` returns `false`
hints: You can check if something is NOT equal to a value, or you can flip a boolean result using a special operator.
Use `!==` to check "not equal to" or `!` before a boolean expression to flip it. Either `str.length !== 0` or `!(str.length === 0)` works.

exercises.title: String Length
exercises.description: Return the length of a given string.
exercises.instructions:
Every string has a `.length` property that tells you how many characters it contains.

Write a function `getLength(str)` that returns the length of the given string.

Examples:
- `getLength("hello")` returns `5`
- `getLength("")` returns `0`

Note: `.length` is a property, not a method — no parentheses needed.
hints: Strings have a built-in property that counts the number of characters, including spaces.
Access the property using dot notation: `str.length`. No parentheses are needed since it is a property, not a method.

exercises.title: Access a Character
exercises.description: Access a specific character in a string using bracket notation.
exercises.instructions:
You can access any character in a string using bracket notation with an index number. Indexes start at `0`, not `1`.

Write a function `firstChar(str)` that returns the first character of the given string.

Examples:
- `firstChar("hello")` returns `"h"`
- `firstChar("JavaScript")` returns `"J"`

The first character is always at index `0`.
hints: Each character in a string has a position number, starting from zero for the first character.
Use square brackets with the index number: `str[0]` gets the first character, `str[1]` gets the second, and so on.

exercises.title: toUpperCase and toLowerCase
exercises.description: Convert a string to uppercase or lowercase.
exercises.instructions:
Strings have methods to change their case:
- `.toUpperCase()` converts all characters to uppercase
- `.toLowerCase()` converts all characters to lowercase

Write a function `shout(str)` that returns the string in all uppercase.

Examples:
- `shout("hello")` returns `"HELLO"`
- `shout("CodeForge")` returns `"CODEFORGE"`

These methods return a new string — the original is not changed.
hints: Strings have a built-in method that converts every character to its uppercase version.
Call `.toUpperCase()` on the string with parentheses: `str.toUpperCase()`. It returns a new string.

exercises.title: String Concatenation
exercises.description: Join two strings together using the concatenation operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `+` operator joins strings together (concatenation). When used with strings, `+` does not add numbers — it combines text.

Write a function `greet(name)` that returns `"Hello, "` followed by the name followed by `"!"`.

Examples:
- `greet("Alice")` returns `"Hello, Alice!"`
- `greet("World")` returns `"Hello, World!"`
hints: The `+` operator does double duty — it adds numbers, but when used with strings, it joins them end-to-end.
Use `+` between string values and variables: `"Hello, " + name + "!"` combines three pieces into one string.

exercises.title: Includes
exercises.description: Check if a string contains a specific substring.
exercises.instructions:
The `.includes()` method checks whether a string contains a specific substring, returning `true` or `false`.

Write a function `hasWord(sentence, word)` that returns `true` if the sentence contains the word.

Examples:
- `hasWord("I love coding", "love")` returns `true`
- `hasWord("I love coding", "hate")` returns `false`

Note: `.includes()` is case-sensitive.
hints: Strings have a built-in method that checks whether one string appears inside another.
Call `.includes()` on the string you want to search, passing the substring to look for: `sentence.includes(word)`.

exercises.title: Basic Interpolation
exercises.description: Insert a variable into a template literal using interpolation.
exercises.instructions:
Template literals use backticks (`` ` ``) instead of quotes. You can insert variables directly into the string using `${variableName}`.

Write a function `welcome(name)` that returns `` `Welcome, ${name}!` ``.

Examples:
- `welcome("Alice")` returns `"Welcome, Alice!"`
- `welcome("Bob")` returns `"Welcome, Bob!"`

This is called string interpolation — it is cleaner than concatenation with `+`.
hints: Template literals use a different kind of quote mark — the backtick character — and allow you to embed variables directly.
Use backticks and `${}` to insert the variable: `` `Welcome, ${name}!` ``. The variable's value replaces the placeholder.

exercises.title: Expression Interpolation
exercises.description: Embed a calculation inside a template literal.
exercises.instructions:
You can put any JavaScript expression inside `${}` — not just variables. Math, function calls, and comparisons all work.

Write a function `priceTag(item, price, quantity)` that returns a string like `"3x Widget = $15"`.

Examples:
- `priceTag("Widget", 5, 3)` returns `"3x Widget = $15"`
- `priceTag("Pen", 2, 10)` returns `"10x Pen = $20"`
hints: Inside `${}` you can write any expression, including math operations. The result is inserted into the string.
Use multiple `${}` blocks in one template literal. Put the multiplication inside: `${price * quantity}`.

exercises.title: Multi-line Strings
exercises.description: Create a multi-line string using template literal backticks.
exercises.instructions:
Template literals preserve line breaks — you can write strings that span multiple lines without any special characters.

Write a function `haiku()` that returns this exact three-line string:
```
Code flows like water
Through the IDE's bright glow
Bugs slowly retreat
```

With regular quotes, you would need `\n` for each line break. Template literals make it natural.
hints: Template literals (backtick strings) preserve actual line breaks in your code as line breaks in the string.
Write the three lines between backticks, pressing Enter between each line. No `\n` characters needed.

exercises.title: Simple If
exercises.description: Use an if statement to return a value based on a condition.
exercises.instructions:
An `if` statement runs code only when a condition is `true`.

Write a function `isPositive(num)` that returns `"yes"` if the number is greater than zero, otherwise returns `"no"`.

Examples:
- `isPositive(5)` returns `"yes"`
- `isPositive(-3)` returns `"no"`
- `isPositive(0)` returns `"no"`
hints: An `if` statement checks a condition in parentheses. If the condition is true, the code inside the curly braces runs.
Write `if (num > 0) { return "yes"; }` and then `return "no";` below it. If the `if` condition is true, the function exits early.

exercises.title: If/Else
exercises.description: Use if/else to return different values for true and false conditions.
exercises.instructions:
An `if/else` statement lets you handle both outcomes of a condition — one block runs when the condition is `true`, the other when it is `false`.

Write a function `ageGroup(age)` that returns `"minor"` if the age is less than 18, otherwise returns `"adult"`.

Examples:
- `ageGroup(15)` returns `"minor"`
- `ageGroup(21)` returns `"adult"`
- `ageGroup(18)` returns `"adult"`
hints: The `else` block runs when the `if` condition is `false`. Together they cover both possible outcomes.
Write `if (age < 18) { return "minor"; } else { return "adult"; }` to handle both cases.

exercises.title: Even or Odd
exercises.description: Check if a number is even or odd using the modulo operator.
exercises.instructions:
A number is even if dividing it by 2 leaves no remainder. You can check this with the modulo operator (`%`).

Write a function `evenOrOdd(num)` that returns `"even"` if the number is even, or `"odd"` if it is odd.

Examples:
- `evenOrOdd(4)` returns `"even"`
- `evenOrOdd(7)` returns `"odd"`
hints: The modulo operator tells you the remainder after division. What remainder does an even number leave when divided by 2?
Check `num % 2 === 0` — if true, the number is even. Otherwise it is odd.

exercises.title: Grade Checker
exercises.description: Return a letter grade based on a numeric score.
exercises.instructions:
Use `if`, `else if`, and `else` to check multiple conditions in order.

Write a function `getGrade(score)` that returns a letter grade:
- 90 or above: `"A"`
- 80 or above: `"B"`
- 70 or above: `"C"`
- 60 or above: `"D"`
- Below 60: `"F"`

Check conditions from highest to lowest. The first match wins.
hints: When you have more than two outcomes, chain multiple conditions using `else if` between the `if` and the final `else`.
Check from highest to lowest: `if (score >= 90)` then `else if (score >= 80)` and so on. The first true condition returns.

exercises.title: Positive, Negative, or Zero
exercises.description: Classify a number as positive, negative, or zero.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `classify(num)` that returns:
- `"positive"` if the number is greater than zero
- `"negative"` if the number is less than zero
- `"zero"` if the number is exactly zero

Examples:
- `classify(5)` returns `"positive"`
- `classify(-3)` returns `"negative"`
- `classify(0)` returns `"zero"`
hints: This requires three possible outcomes, so you need an `if`, an `else if`, and an `else`.
Check `num > 0` first, then `num < 0`, and the `else` handles the remaining case (zero).

exercises.title: Voting Age
exercises.description: Check if a person meets the minimum voting age.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `canVoteMessage(age)` that returns:
- `"You can vote!"` if the person is 18 or older
- `"You cannot vote yet."` if the person is under 18

Examples:
- `canVoteMessage(21)` returns `"You can vote!"`
- `canVoteMessage(16)` returns `"You cannot vote yet."`
hints: Compare the age to the minimum using a comparison operator that includes the boundary value.
Use `>=` (greater than or equal to) to check if the age meets the minimum of 18.

exercises.title: Switch Statement
exercises.description: Use a switch statement to match a value to one of several cases.
exercises.instructions:
A `switch` statement compares a value against several `case` labels. When a match is found, the code for that case runs. The `default` case runs if nothing matches.

Write a function called `getActivity` that takes a string `day` and returns the matching activity:
- `"Monday"` → `"Gym"`
- `"Tuesday"` → `"Study"`
- `"Wednesday"` → `"Cook"`
- For any other day → `"Rest"`

Use a `switch` statement (not if/else).

Example: `getActivity("Monday")` returns `"Gym"`
Example: `getActivity("Friday")` returns `"Rest"`
hints: A switch statement starts with `switch (value) {` and each case starts with `case "value":` followed by the code to run.
Write `switch (day) { case "Monday": return "Gym"; case "Tuesday": return "Study"; ... default: return "Rest"; }`.

exercises.title: Ternary Operator
exercises.description: Use the ternary operator to choose between two values in one line.
exercises.instructions:
The ternary operator is a shorthand for if/else that fits on one line:

`condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`

Write a function called `classify` that takes a number `age` and returns `"adult"` if the age is 18 or older, otherwise `"minor"`.

Use a ternary operator (not if/else).

Example: `classify(21)` returns `"adult"`
Example: `classify(15)` returns `"minor"`
hints: The ternary operator has three parts: the condition, then `?`, then the value for true, then `:`, then the value for false.
Write `return age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";` to return one value or the other based on the condition.

exercises.title: Counting Loop
exercises.description: Use a for loop to build a string of numbers from 1 to n.
exercises.instructions:
A `for` loop repeats code a specific number of times. It has three parts: initialization, condition, and update.

Write a function `countTo(n)` that returns a string of numbers from 1 to n, separated by commas.

Examples:
- `countTo(3)` returns `"1,2,3"`
- `countTo(5)` returns `"1,2,3,4,5"`

Use a `for` loop starting at 1 and going up to n.
hints: A `for` loop has three parts in parentheses: where to start, when to stop, and how to step forward.
Use `for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++)` to count from 1 to n. Build a string by adding each number and a comma separator.

exercises.title: Sum to N
exercises.description: Use a for loop to calculate the sum of numbers from 1 to n.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `sumTo(n)` that adds up all numbers from 1 to n using a `for` loop.

Examples:
- `sumTo(5)` returns `15` (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5)
- `sumTo(10)` returns `55`
- `sumTo(1)` returns `1`

Start with a total of 0 and add each number to it inside the loop.
hints: Create a variable to hold the running total, then add each number to it as the loop iterates.
Start with `let total = 0;` then inside the loop body: `total = total + i;`. Return the total after the loop ends.

exercises.title: Loop Through Array
exercises.description: Use a for loop to process each item in an array.
exercises.instructions:
Arrays store lists of values. You can loop through them using a `for` loop with the array's `.length` property.

Write a function `sumArray(numbers)` that returns the sum of all numbers in the array.

Examples:
- `sumArray([1, 2, 3])` returns `6`
- `sumArray([10, 20, 30])` returns `60`

Use `numbers[i]` to access each element and `numbers.length` to know when to stop.
hints: Array indexes start at 0 and go up to one less than the array's length. Use `.length` to control the loop.
Use `for (let i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++)` and access each element with `numbers[i]`.

exercises.title: While Loop
exercises.description: Use a while loop to repeat code until a condition is false.
exercises.instructions:
A `while` loop keeps running as long as its condition is `true`. Use it when you do not know in advance how many times to loop.

Write a function `doubleUntil(start, limit)` that keeps doubling `start` until it reaches or exceeds `limit`, then returns the result.

Examples:
- `doubleUntil(1, 10)` returns `16` (1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16)
- `doubleUntil(3, 20)` returns `24` (3 → 6 → 12 → 24)
hints: A `while` loop checks its condition before each iteration. If the condition is false from the start, the loop body never runs.
Use `while (value < limit)` and multiply the value by 2 inside the loop. Return the value after the loop finishes.

exercises.title: Countdown
exercises.description: Count down from n to 1 using a loop.
exercises.instructions:
Loops can count downward by using a decrementing update (`i--`).

Write a function `countdown(n)` that returns a string counting down from n to 1, separated by commas.

Examples:
- `countdown(5)` returns `"5,4,3,2,1"`
- `countdown(3)` returns `"3,2,1"`
hints: A for loop can start high and count down by using `--` (decrement) instead of `++` in the update part.
Use `for (let i = n; i >= 1; i--)` to count downward. Build the result string like the counting loop exercise.

exercises.title: Repeat String
exercises.description: Repeat a string n times using a loop.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `repeatStr(str, n)` that returns the string repeated `n` times.

Examples:
- `repeatStr("ha", 3)` returns `"hahaha"`
- `repeatStr("ab", 2)` returns `"abab"`
- `repeatStr("x", 5)` returns `"xxxxx"`

Build the result by concatenating the string in each loop iteration.
hints: Start with an empty string and use a loop that runs exactly n times, adding the input string each iteration.
Use `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` and concatenate: `result = result + str;` inside the loop.

exercises.title: String to Number
exercises.description: Convert a string to a number using the Number function.
exercises.instructions:
The `Number()` function converts a value to a number. This is useful when you receive input as text but need to do math with it.

Write a function `addStrings(a, b)` that takes two string numbers, converts them to actual numbers, and returns their sum.

Examples:
- `addStrings("5", "3")` returns `8`
- `addStrings("10", "20")` returns `30`

Without conversion, `"5" + "3"` would give `"53"` (string concatenation)!
hints: There is a built-in function that converts a string representation of a number into an actual number value.
Wrap each string in `Number()` to convert it: `Number("5")` gives the number `5`. Then use `+` to add them.

exercises.title: Number to String
exercises.description: Convert a number to a string using the String function.
exercises.instructions:
The `String()` function converts any value to a string. This is useful when you need to combine numbers with text.

Write a function `labeledScore(name, score)` that returns a string like `"Alice: 95"` using `String()` to convert the score.

Examples:
- `labeledScore("Alice", 95)` returns `"Alice: 95"`
- `labeledScore("Bob", 80)` returns `"Bob: 80"`
hints: There is a built-in function that converts any value to its string representation.
Use `String(score)` to convert the number, then concatenate the pieces: `name + ": " + String(score)`.

exercises.title: Temperature Converter
exercises.description: Convert a temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `toCelsius(fahrenheit)` that converts a Fahrenheit temperature to Celsius.

Formula: `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9`

Examples:
- `toCelsius(32)` returns `0`
- `toCelsius(212)` returns `100`

exercises.title: Tip Calculator
exercises.description: Calculate a tip amount from a bill and tip percentage.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `calculateTip(bill, tipPercent)` that returns the tip amount.

The tip is calculated by multiplying the bill by the tip percentage divided by 100.

exercises.title: Relative Positioning
exercises.description: Nudge an element from its normal position using position relative.
exercises.instructions:
The `position: relative` property lets you move an element from where it would normally appear. Use `top`, `right`, `bottom`, or `left` to offset it.

Style the `.nudged` element:
- Set `position` to `relative`
- Set `top` to `20px` (pushes it down 20px from its normal position)
- Set `left` to `10px` (pushes it right 10px from its normal position)

The element still takes up its original space in the layout — it just renders shifted.

Set `position: relative` first, then use `top` and `left` to specify how far to shift. Positive `top` moves down, positive `left` moves right.

exercises.title: Absolute Positioning
exercises.description: Position an element precisely within a relative parent.
exercises.instructions:
An element with `position: absolute` is removed from the normal flow and positioned relative to its nearest positioned ancestor (a parent with `position: relative`).

The HTML has a `.container` (already set to `position: relative`) and a `.badge` inside it.

Style the `.badge` element:
- Set `position` to `absolute`
- Set `top` to `0`
- Set `right` to `0`

This pins the badge to the top-right corner of the container.

New

exercises.title: Fixed Header
exercises.description: Create a header that stays fixed at the top of the viewport.
exercises.instructions:
An element with `position: fixed` stays in the same position on screen even when the user scrolls. This is commonly used for navigation bars.

Style the `.header` element:

- Set `top` to `0`
- Set `left` to `0`
- Set `width` to `100%`
- Set `background-color` to `#1e293b`
- Set `color` to `white`

Fixed elements are removed from the document flow, so content may appear behind them.

exercises.title: Enable Flexbox
exercises.description: Apply display flex to a container to enable flexbox layout.
exercises.instructions:
Flexbox is a layout system that arranges items in a row or column. To use it, set `display: flex` on the container element.

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`

Once flexbox is enabled, its children automatically arrange in a horizontal row. Without flexbox, block elements stack vertically.

Item 1
Item 2
Item 3

exercises.title: Flex Direction
exercises.description: Arrange flex items in a row or column using flex-direction.
exercises.instructions:
The `flex-direction` property controls whether flex items arrange horizontally (`row`) or vertically (`column`).

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `flex-direction` to `column`

The default direction is `row` (horizontal). Changing to `column` stacks items vertically, like a list.

Top
Middle
Bottom

exercises.title: Justify Content
exercises.description: Distribute flex items along the main axis using justify-content.
exercises.instructions:
The `justify-content` property controls how items are distributed along the main axis (horizontally in a row, vertically in a column).

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `justify-content` to `space-between`

Common values: `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around`, `space-evenly`.

`space-between` puts equal space between items, with the first and last items flush against the edges.

Left
Center
Right

The property is `justify-content`. The value `space-between` pushes the first item to the start and the last to the end, with equal gaps between.

exercises.title: Align Items
exercises.description: Align flex items along the cross axis using align-items.
exercises.instructions:
The `align-items` property controls how items are aligned along the cross axis (vertical in a row, horizontal in a column).

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `align-items` to `center`
- Set `height` to `150px` (so there is space to see the vertical alignment)

Common values: `stretch` (default), `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, `baseline`.
exercises.providedHtml:
Short
Taller
Short

The property is `align-items`. Set it to `center` to vertically center items when flex-direction is row.

exercises.title: Gap
exercises.description: Add space between flex items using the gap property.
exercises.instructions:
The `gap` property adds space between flex items without needing margins. It only creates space between items, not around the outer edges.

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `gap` to `16px`

The `gap` property is cleaner than margins because it does not add extra space before the first item or after the last.

The property is `gap`. Set it to a pixel value to add uniform spacing between all flex items.

exercises.description: Apply display grid and define columns to create a grid layout.

CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system. To use it, set `display: grid` on the container and define columns with `grid-template-columns`.

Style the `.grid` element:
- Set `display` to `grid`
- Set `grid-template-columns` to `200px 200px 200px` (three equal columns)

exercises.title: Grid Columns
exercises.description: Use grid-template-columns with different widths to create varied columns.
exercises.instructions:
The `grid-template-columns` property accepts different widths for each column.

Style the `.grid` element:
- Set `display` to `grid`
- Set `grid-template-columns` to `100px 200px 100px` (narrow, wide, narrow)

exercises.description: Define explicit row heights in a CSS Grid layout.

The `grid-template-rows` property defines the height of each row in the grid.

Style the `.grid` element:

exercises.title: Viewport Meta
exercises.description: Add the viewport meta tag to make a page mobile-friendly.
exercises.instructions:
Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render pages at a desktop width and then zoom out, making text tiny. The viewport meta tag tells the browser to match the device width.

Add a `<meta>` tag inside `<head>` with:
- `name` set to `"viewport"`
- `content` set to `"width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"`

This single tag is the foundation of responsive web design. Every modern web page should include it.

Mobile-Friendly Page

exercises.title: Fluid Widths
exercises.description: Use percentages and max-width for fluid, responsive sizing.
exercises.instructions:
Fixed pixel widths break on smaller screens. Using percentages with `max-width` creates fluid layouts that adapt to any screen size.

Style the `.content` element:
- Set `width` to `100%`
- Set `max-width` to `600px`
- Set `margin` to `0 auto` (to center it)

Responsive Content

Set `width: 100%` so it fills small screens, `max-width: 600px` to cap the width, and `margin: 0 auto` to center it.

exercises.title: Define a Custom Property
exercises.description: Create a CSS custom property on the root element.
exercises.instructions:
CSS custom properties (also called CSS variables) let you store values and reuse them throughout your stylesheet. They always start with two dashes (`--`).

Define a custom property on `:root`:
- `--primary-color` with the value `#3b82f6`

Then style the `.box` element:
- Set `background-color` to use the custom property with `var(--primary-color)`

The `:root` selector targets the document root, making the variable available everywhere.

hints: Custom properties are defined with two dashes at the start of the name and are declared inside a rule block.
Define the variable inside `:root { --primary-color: #3b82f6; }` then reference it with `var(--primary-color)`.

exercises.title: Use Multiple Variables
exercises.description: Apply multiple CSS custom properties to style an element.
exercises.instructions:
Custom properties shine when you define a set of related values and reuse them across your styles.

Define these custom properties on `:root`:
- `--bg-dark` with value `#1e293b`
- `--text-light` with value `#f1f5f9`

Then style the `.card` element:
- Set `background-color` using `var(--bg-dark)`
- Set `color` using `var(--text-light)`

This pattern is the foundation of CSS theming.

Dark Card

Styled with CSS custom properties.

Each variable follows the pattern `--name: value;`. Reference them with `var(--name)` as the property value.

exercises.title: Box Shadow
exercises.description: Add a shadow effect to an element using box-shadow.

The `box-shadow` property adds a shadow effect around an element's frame. The values are: `x-offset y-offset blur-radius color`.

- Add a `box-shadow` of `0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15)`

This creates a subtle shadow below the card (0px horizontal offset, 2px down, 8px blur, with 15% black).

Shadows add depth and make elements feel like they float above the page.

Style the `h1` element:
- Add a `text-shadow` of `2px 2px 4px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3)`
- Set `color` to `#1e40af`

Text shadows can make headings stand out or create visual depth.
